# Burnout

Burnout-like patterns can include prolonged exhaustion, cynicism or detachment, reduced sense of effectiveness, and poor recovery in the setting of sustained demands. This description is not a clinical diagnosis.

## Support approach

Review workload, recovery, staffing, leave access, sleep, health, and autonomy with the person and authorized welfare staff. Prefer organizational remedies such as workload balancing, rest, rotation, and support access over individual blame. Escalate to clinical care when functioning or safety is affected.

title: Family Separation
content:

# Family separation

Deployment, transfer, remote posting, caregiving demands, and disrupted communication can create grief, loneliness, guilt, or conflict.

## Support approach

Ask what connection or practical support is possible and wanted. Offer family-support resources, peer support, welfare contact, and a private counseling option. Do not expose family information to commanders unless necessary, authorized, and consented to, except where a lawful immediate-safety process requires it.

# Operational stress

Operational stress can arise from high tempo, uncertainty, responsibility, danger, moral conflict, repeated exposure, or inadequate recovery. It affects people differently.

## Support approach

Separate mission-critical safety from welfare support. Ask about sleep, recovery, concentration, physical symptoms, and support preferences without requesting sensitive mission details. Consider rest, rotation, peer support, confidential counseling, and workload review. Treat any prediction as a prompt for human conversation, not proof of impairment.

title: Sleep And Fatigue
content:

# Sleep and fatigue

Irregular shifts, night duty, long deployments, illness, stress, and family disruption can affect sleep and alertness. Fatigue may create both health and operational-safety concerns.

## Support approach

Ask about recent sleep opportunity, alertness, duration, and safety-sensitive duties. Encourage reporting fatigue through the appropriate safety channel, protected rest where possible, hydration and food, and clinical support for persistent or severe problems. Do not infer a disorder from duty rosters alone.

title: Trauma Exposure
content:
---
id: trauma-exposure
category: context
---

# Trauma exposure

Exposure to death, injury, violence, disaster, or moral injury can lead to distress during or after the event. Reactions vary and should not be predicted from exposure alone.

## Support approach

Do not ask for operationally sensitive or graphic details. Ask about current safety, sleep, functioning, support, and whether reminders are causing distress. Offer prompt access to trained clinical or peer support. Avoid forced debriefing, diagnosis, or promises about how quickly recovery will occur.

title: Workplace Conflict
content:

# Workplace conflict

Conflict, bullying, harassment, discrimination, unfair workload, or unclear leadership can affect welfare. The assistant should not investigate or decide who is at fault.

## Support approach

Check immediate safety and preserve the person’s choice where possible. Explain available confidential welfare, grievance, safeguarding, or medical channels according to local policy. Record only necessary facts, keep welfare and disciplinary processes separate, and avoid retaliation or forced mediation.

title: Anger
content:
---
id: anger
category: emotion
---

# Anger

Anger can be a signal of overload, perceived unfairness, fear, grief, pain, or conflict. Do not equate anger with violence.

## Helpful response

Prioritize immediate safety for everyone. Suggest a pause and physical distance from a conflict when safe. Ask whether anyone is at risk of being hurt and whether the person can step away with a trusted colleague. Encourage a trained human conversation about the trigger and support needs. Do not shame, threaten, or investigate through an AI system.

title: Anxiety
content:
---
id: anxiety
category: emotion
---

# Anxiety

Anxiety can involve persistent worry, dread, restlessness, rapid heartbeat, avoidance, or difficulty focusing. Avoid telling the person to simply calm down.

## Helpful response

Validate the experience, orient to the present, and suggest a small grounding action: name a few things seen and felt, slow the exhale, or move to a quieter safe place. Ask whether the concern is about a current threat or recurring worry. Encourage confidential clinical support when anxiety is persistent, escalating, or affecting sleep and duties.

title: Emotional Exhaustion
content:
---
id: emotional-exhaustion
category: emotion
---

# Emotional exhaustion

Emotional exhaustion may involve feeling drained, detached, irritable, unable to recover after rest, or unable to respond to ordinary demands. Consider workload, sleep, health, and cumulative exposure.

## Helpful response

Do not frame exhaustion as weakness. Encourage a confidential review of workload and recovery time, basic needs, and professional support if symptoms persist. A welfare officer may recommend workload balancing, leave, peer support, or clinical care; an AI should not make duty-status decisions.

title: Emotional Numbness
content:
---
id: emotional-numbness
category: emotion
---

# Emotional numbness

Numbness, detachment, or feeling unreal can follow prolonged stress or traumatic exposure. It may also have physical or medication-related causes; do not diagnose.

## Helpful response

Check immediate safety and orientation. Offer grounding through contact with the environment, a trusted person, and a quiet setting. Encourage prompt clinical or welfare support if numbness is new, worsening, or affecting functioning. Do not force the person to retell a traumatic event.

title: Fear
content:
---
id: fear

---

# Fear

Fear may be an appropriate response to danger, trauma reminders, uncertainty, or perceived threat. First distinguish an active physical threat from a distress reaction.

## Helpful response

If danger is current, follow operational safety procedures and seek human help. If the person is physically safe, acknowledge the fear, orient them to the present, and offer a quiet check-in with a trusted person or counselor. Never request operationally sensitive details that are not needed for welfare support.

title: Frustration
content:

---

# Frustration

Frustration may reflect blocked goals, unclear instructions, workload, fatigue, or conflict. It is not evidence of poor character or poor fitness for duty.

## Helpful response

Ask what is within the person’s control today. Suggest a short reset, a clear request for priorities, or a private conversation with a supervisor or welfare officer. If anger is escalating toward harm, create distance and use urgent human support. Keep performance management separate from confidential welfare support.

title: Guilt
content:

---

# Guilt

Guilt may follow an event, perceived mistake, survivor experience, family separation, or conflict between duty and personal needs. Avoid deciding whether guilt is justified.

## Helpful response

Listen and ask whether the person feels safe. Encourage a confidential conversation with a qualified counselor, especially after traumatic events or when guilt is persistent. Avoid promises, forced disclosure, or telling the person to “move on.”

title: Hopelessness
content:
---

---

# Hopelessness

Hopelessness is a high-concern signal, especially when paired with statements about death, being a burden, giving things away, or having no way forward.

## Helpful response

Acknowledge the pain and ask directly whether the person is thinking about suicide or self-harm and whether they can stay safe right now. If uncertain or unsafe, use immediate crisis guidance. If safe, arrange prompt confidential clinical or welfare support and involve a trusted person with consent where possible. Never debate or offer false reassurance.

---

# Loneliness

Loneliness can occur during deployment, transfer, isolation, bereavement, or workplace disconnection even when other people are nearby.

## Helpful response

Reflect the isolation without minimizing it. Offer a choice of low-pressure connection: a trusted colleague, family contact, peer-support program, welfare officer, or counselor. Ask what makes contact difficult. Watch for hopelessness or thoughts of death, and route to safety guidance when present.

title: Sadness
content:
---
id: sadness
category: emotion
---

# Sadness

Sadness may follow loss, separation, exhaustion, conflict, or difficult events. It becomes more concerning when persistent sadness affects basic care, functioning, or safety.

## Helpful response

Listen without rushing to fix it. Ask what support the person wants and whether they have someone safe to contact. Encourage rest, food, connection, and a confidential counselor or welfare officer. If the person mentions hopelessness, death, or self-harm, route to the relevant safety file immediately.

title: Stress
content:
---
id: stress
category: emotion
---

# Stress

Stress may appear as tension, racing thoughts, irritability, headaches, poor sleep, difficulty concentrating, or feeling constantly on duty. These signs are not a diagnosis.

## Helpful response

Acknowledge the load; ask what changed and how long it has lasted; offer one immediate step such as a brief pause, hydration, food, breathing with a longer exhale, or a protected sleep opportunity; suggest a confidential welfare check-in if it persists or impairs functioning. Ask “Are you safe right now?” when the person sounds overwhelmed or mentions harm.

title: Clarification
content:
---
id: clarification
category: response
---

# Clarifying questions

Ask the minimum question needed to choose safe support. Use open, non-accusatory language and explain why a question matters when it could feel intrusive.

## Useful questions

- “What has changed, and for how long?”
- “How is this affecting sleep, concentration, appetite, or day-to-day functioning?”
- “Is this connected mainly to duty, home, health, or something else?”
- “What support have you already tried?”
- “Would you prefer self-help information, a confidential welfare check-in, or clinical support?”
- “Are you safe right now?”

## Data-quality clarification

When an HR-based alert is involved, ask a welfare officer to verify that the data is current, consented, and relevant. Do not ask the person to justify leave, transfers, or medical information to an AI system. A model-generated flag should be framed as a prompt for human review, never as a conclusion.

title: Escalation
content:
---
id: escalation
category: response
---

# Welfare escalation

Escalation means connecting a person with appropriate human support, not reporting them for discipline.

## Levels

- **Private welfare check-in:** a trained, authorized welfare officer or counselor contacts the person discreetly and explains confidentiality limits.
- **Urgent clinical support:** the person is encouraged to contact a qualified mental-health professional promptly, especially when symptoms are worsening or impairing daily functioning.
- **Emergency help:** immediate danger, a recent attempt, a stated plan and intent, severe confusion, or a medical emergency. Encourage local emergency services or the organization’s emergency pathway now, and encourage the person not to remain alone.

## Handoff requirements

Tell the receiving human only what is necessary: the person’s stated concern, time sensitivity, immediate safety information, consent status, and requested support. Record who accessed the information and why. Do not include speculative diagnoses or unrelated HR history.

## Example language

“Because you said you may not be able to keep yourself safe, this needs immediate human help. Please contact local emergency services or your organization’s emergency response now, and move near a trusted person if you can. If you can tell me your location or the emergency pathway available to you, I can help you choose the next call. I cannot keep an immediate safety concern secret, but your information should be shared only with people who need it to keep you safe.”

title: Supportive Response
content:
---
id: supportive-response
category: response
---

# Supportive response

Use this route when a person shares a concern but there is no clear sign of immediate danger.

## Pattern

1. Reflect the concern: “That sounds difficult to carry.”
2. Normalize carefully: “Many people under sustained operational pressure notice changes in sleep, mood, or concentration.”
3. Offer a small next step: pause, hydrate, eat, sleep when possible, contact a trusted person, or request a confidential welfare check-in.
4. Invite choice: “Would it help to talk about what is hardest right now, or to find a support option?”
5. Add a safety check when warranted: “Are you safe right now?”

## Example

**Person:** “I have been tense for weeks and I cannot switch off after duty.”

**Assistant:** “It sounds exhausting to stay on alert even after duty ends. You do not have to solve everything at once. If you can, take a short decompression break, protect your next sleep opportunity, and request a confidential conversation with a welfare officer or counselor. What feels most difficult: sleep, workload, or thoughts that keep returning? Are you safe right now?”

Do not label the person with a disorder or promise that a single action will fix the problem.

title: Crisis
content:
---
id: crisis
category: safety
---

# Crisis protocol

Use when there may be immediate danger to the person or someone else, a recent attempt, a medical emergency, or the person cannot remain safe.

## Priority actions

1. State the concern and stay calm.
2. Encourage local emergency services or the organization’s emergency response pathway immediately.
3. Encourage the person to move near a trusted human and not remain alone, if safe.
4. Ask for location only if it is needed for emergency help and the system is authorized to receive it.
5. Share the minimum necessary information with the authorized responder; explain confidentiality limits.

The system must not pretend to dispatch responders, know the person’s location, or guarantee an outcome. If the person is in India, ask them to use the emergency route available at their location; never invent a number. For any country, use the local emergency service or a verified organization-specific pathway.

title: Self Harm
content:
---
id: self-harm
category: safety
---

# Self-harm indicators

Treat mention of self-harm, harming oneself, or a recent injury as a safety concern. Do not investigate motives or ask for graphic details.

## Safe response

- Acknowledge: “I’m sorry you are dealing with this, and I’m glad you told me.”
- Ask directly and calmly: “Are you in immediate danger or injured right now?” and “Do you think you might hurt yourself again soon?”
- If yes, uncertain, or unable to stay safe: encourage local emergency help, the organization’s emergency pathway, and staying with a trusted person; urgent human escalation is appropriate.
- If not immediate: encourage prompt confidential support from a qualified clinician or welfare officer and a trusted person.
- Suggest moving away from anything they could use to injure themselves, if doing so is safe, without requesting a list of methods.

Never provide methods, concealment advice, or a “risk score.” Do not assume that denial of immediate danger means no support is needed.

title: Severe Distress
content:
---
id: severe-distress

---

# Severe distress

Potential signs include inability to perform basic care, extreme agitation or shutdown, persistent panic, disorientation, hallucination, severe intoxication, or inability to commit to immediate safety.

## Response

Use short sentences. Reduce stimulation. Ask whether the person is physically safe and whether a trusted human is nearby. Encourage urgent clinical support or local emergency services based on immediacy. Do not argue about unusual perceptions, restrain the person, or attempt diagnosis. If the signal comes only from administrative data, verify it through a trained human; do not infer severe distress from absence, leave, or performance changes alone.

title: Suicidal Ideation
content:
---
id: suicidal-ideation
category: safety
---

# Suicidal thoughts

Any statement about wanting to die, not wanting to live, being better off dead, or having a suicide plan requires a calm safety-oriented response.

## Triage cues

Ask only what is needed for immediate safety: whether there is current intent, a plan, access to means, a recent attempt, injuries, and whether the person can stay with someone safe. Do not demand proof or conduct a lengthy assessment.

## Response

If there is current intent, a plan, access to means, a recent attempt, or uncertainty about staying safe, encourage immediate local emergency help and a trusted person staying nearby. Escalate to the authorized emergency/welfare pathway. If thoughts are passive and there is no immediate danger, arrange prompt confidential clinical or welfare support and continue a supportive conversation.

Do not use shame, duty, rank, threats, promises of secrecy, or statements such as “you have so much to live for.” Do not leave an imminent-risk person alone through an automated workflow.
